bib.title: Multi-News: a Large-Scale Multi-Document Summarization Dataset and Abstractive Hierarchical Model
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2019), pages 1074-1084

question: Can a large-scale multi-document news summarization dataset be built, and how do extractive and neural abstractive systems (including an MMR-augmented pointer-generator) perform on it?
hypothesis: Data sparsity is the bottleneck for neural MDS; a large dataset plus an end-to-end MMR-in-attention model should help, and learned similarity/redundancy parameters should reduce redundancy.
contributions: Introduce Multi-News, the first large-scale multi-document summarization dataset in the news domain (56,216 article-summary pairs)
Propose Hi-MAP, an end-to-end method incorporating MMR into a pointer-generator network
Benchmark various methods on the dataset to lay foundations for future work on large-scale MDS

method.summary: Dataset of newser.com editor-written summaries linked to cited source articles (2 to 10 per summary), collected via Wayback links. Models truncate the concatenated sources to 500 tokens and are compared with extractive baselines using ROUGE and a small Best-Worst Scaling human study. Hi-MAP adds a sentence-level LSTM and a learned MMR score that rescales word-level pointer-generator attention.

datasets.name: Multi-News
datasets.size: 56,216 article-summary pairs; avg 2,103.49 words per concatenated input, 263.66 words per summary, 9.97 summary sentences, vocab 666,515
datasets.source: newser.com; summaries written by professional editors with links to cited original articles; 20 editors wrote 85% of summaries; over 1,500 source sites appear 5+ times. Over 250,000 Wayback links collected; only examples with 2 to 10 sources kept
datasets.preprocessing: Downloaded and processed cited articles to text; examples with more than 10 sources dropped. Source counts per example: 2:23,894; 3:12,707; 4:5,022; 5:1,873; 6:763; 7:382; 8:209; 9:89; 10:33

datasets.name: CNN/Daily Mail
datasets.split: train/val/test; used to train models later tested on DUC 2004

models.name: Hi-MAP (Hierarchical MMR-Attention Pointer-generator)
models.architecture: pointer-generator with 1-layer Bi-LSTM word encoder, sentence-level LSTM, learned MMR scores multiplied into word attention

models.name: PG-BRNN
models.architecture: OpenNMT pointer-generator, 1-layer bi-LSTM encoder, single-layer LSTM decoder
models.hidden: 128-dim word embeddings, 256-dim hidden per direction, 512-dim decoder

other.note: run without bottom-up masked attention; pretrained by OpenNMT on CNNDM for DUC

models.name: CopyTransformer
models.architecture: Transformer encoder-decoder with copy mechanism (Gehrmann et al. 2018), one randomly chosen attention head as copy distribution

models.name: PG-Original / PG-MMR
models.architecture: pointer-generator; PG-MMR applies MMR on top of pretrained PG-Original

other.note: DUC numbers copied from Lebanoff et al. 2018; for Multi-News, PG-MMR corresponds to 'PG-MMR w Cosine' with their sentence regression model trained on Multi-News

training.seq_len: 500 tokens input (first 500/S tokens from each of S source documents, quota redistributed iteratively when a source is shorter; special token between documents)

other.note: No optimizer, learning rate, batch size, steps or hardware reported.

parameters.extractive_output_length: 100 tokens for DUC, 300 tokens for Multi-News
parameters.First-k: first k sentences from each source article; only First-1 for DUC

metrics.name: ROUGE R-1, R-2, R-SU
metrics.definition: overlap of unigrams, bigrams, and skip bigrams with max distance four words (Lin 2004)

metrics.name: Best-Worst Scaling counts
metrics.definition: number of times a system was chosen best in pairwise comparisons on informativeness, fluency, non-redundancy

metrics.name: % novel n-grams
metrics.definition: percentage of gold-summary n-grams not in the input documents

metrics.name: extractive fragment coverage / density / compression
metrics.definition: Grusky et al. 2018 measures; sources concatenated into one input

eval.protocol: ROUGE on DUC 2004 (models trained on CNNDM, as Lebanoff et al. 2018) and Multi-News test. Human eval: 3 native English speaker annotators, 50 random test documents, all pairs of 4 systems (PG-MMR, CopyTransformer, Hi-MAP, gold), randomised order; one-way ANOVA with Tukey HSD, p 0.05. No ROUGE variance or seeds reported.

availability.data: Wayback-archived links and scripts to reproduce the dataset released (not the article text itself)

evidence.quote: We split our dataset into training (80%, 44,972), validation (10%, 5,622), and test (10%, 5,622) sets.

results.claim: Multi-News contains 56,216 article-summary pairs, about two orders of magnitude more than prior MDS news data.
Multi-News summaries average about 264 words, far longer than CNNDM.
results.note: Text says about 260 words on average

results.claim: Gold summaries are about as abstractive as CNNDM: 17.76% of unigrams are novel.
results.setup: Table 4, percentage of summary n-grams absent from inputs

results.claim: Trained and tested on Multi-News, CopyTransformer gets the best R-1 and Hi-MAP the best R-2.
results.setup: Multi-News test, inputs truncated to 500 tokens, trained on Multi-News train; single run
results.table: Table 6, row Hi-MAP (Our Model), column R-2
results.note: CopyTransformer R-1 43.57 vs Hi-MAP 43.47; R-SU 17.37 vs 17.41

results.claim: A strong extractive baseline, First-3, reaches R-1 39.41 on Multi-News, beating LexRank, TextRank and MMR.
results.setup: Multi-News test; extractive outputs of 300 tokens

results.claim: On DUC 2004 with models trained on CNNDM, PG-MMR is best on R-1 and Hi-MAP is competitive.
results.table: Table 5, row Hi-MAP (Our Model), column R-1
results.note: LexRank R-1 35.56; PG-MMR numbers copied from Lebanoff et al. 2018

results.claim: In human pairwise comparison Hi-MAP is chosen best for non-redundancy 100 times versus 45 for PG-MMR, but CopyTransformer scores 107.
results.setup: 50 random Multi-News test documents, 3 annotators, all pairs of PG-MMR, CopyTransformer, Hi-MAP, Human

results.claim: Feeding 500 tokens of LexRank/TextRank/MMR extractive output into the abstractive model did not improve results; authors attribute it to the truncated input mirroring First-3.
results.setup: DUC and Multi-News; numbers not given

results.claim: Training on Multi-News and testing on DUC gave no significant improvement; low DUC performance blamed on domain differences.
results.setup: Multi-News to DUC transfer; numbers not given

limits: Inputs truncated to 500 tokens (about 500/S per source) and concatenated, reducing MDS to SDS; avg input is 2,103 words so most source text is unseen; longer inputs and cross-document modelling are left to future work.
Training hyperparameters (optimizer, lr, batch size, steps, hardware, seeds) are not reported; single-run ROUGE with no variance.
Human evaluation is small: 50 documents, 3 annotators; CopyTransformer beats Hi-MAP on informativeness and fluency in Table 7.
Only a few non-neural baselines tested; other classical methods left to future work (footnote 3).
Dataset article text is not redistributed, only Wayback links and scripts, so reproduction depends on archive availability.
Pre-2019 models only (LSTM pointer-generator, small Transformer); no pretrained LMs. Dated by later work.

terms.definition: the percentage of words in the summary that are from the source article, measuring the extent to which a summary is derivative of a text
the average length of the extractive fragment to which each summary word belongs
the word ratio between the articles and its summaries
Maximal Marginal Relevance, an approach for combining query-relevance with information-novelty in the context of summarization
